newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM brings back old guard for "new age".
newsitem.headline: Japan PM brings back old guard for "new age".

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto launched his new minority government on Thursday by naming a low-key cabinet of mainly party elders which included a 69-year-old finance minister.

There were no ministers under the age of 50 and only one woman in a 20-member cabinet which for the first time in three years was made up solely of members of Hashimoto's long-ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP).

"This cabinet is designed to meet the demands of a new age," Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama said after announcing the new cabinet. "Our most important tasks are fiscal and administrative reform."

Hashimoto picked one of the LDP's key power brokers, Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, as his finance minister. He charged him with keeping Japan's sluggish economic recovery going and at the same time streamlining a bloated and over-zealous bureaucracy.
The key task for Mitsuzuka, a former trade minister and LDP secretary-general, is to cut the ministry's power by creating a new body to oversee banks and other financial institutions.
The sector has been hit by a series of scandals involving senior bureaucrats and mishandling of Japan's financial woes.
Asked how he will cut bureaucrats' power, Mitsuzuka said: "Pure confrontation will be bad, but I'll say what I must say."

Several hours before naming the cabinet, Hashimoto was formally elected prime minister by parliament, avoiding the embarrassment of going through a second round of voting when his old allies, now out of government, voted for him.
He received 262 votes in the 500-member Lower House on the strength of a loose alliance the LDP has formed with its old allies, the Social Democrats and the tiny Sakigake party.

But Hashimoto, prime minister since last January, in effect leads a minority government because the LDP won only 239 seats -- 12 short of a majority -- in October 20 elections. The coalition partners then did not renew formal ties with the LDP.
Kajiyama, who also doubles as government spokesman, and Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda were the only ministers to retain their posts from the old cabinet which had included coalition members.
Ikeda was kept because of a pressing foreign policy schedule, including key meetings with his counterparts from Russia, China and the United States later this month.

Ikeda's challenges include cementing a new security arrangement with the United States and mending ties with China marred by a rows over disputed islands and Hashimoto's visit to a controversial war shrine.
The cabinet was dominated by so-called "veteran" or "old-style" LDP politicians, mostly in their 60s and 70s, including Finance Minister Mitsuzuka, Trade Minister Shinji Sato and spokesman Kajiyama.

The only politician considered a reformer was Health Minister Junichiro Koizumi, an outspoken lawmaker who as a former posts and telecommunications minister first started moves to privatise the government's postal service.
In their first brief news conferences, the new ministers all pledged to carry out government reforms.
"Deregulation is the most important topic," said new trade minister Sato, a son of 1960s prime minister Eisaku Sato.

The average age of the new cabinet went up 1.4 years from the previous cabinet to 62.7 years. The youngest is Home Affairs Minister Katsuhiko Shirakawa, 51, and the oldest is Justice Minister Isao Matsuura at 73.
The only woman is Environment Minister Michiko Ishii, 63, a pharmacist known for her work in medicine and welfare.
